title: Plaque as a Community, Not Debris
topic: the oral microbiome and the biofilm model of dental caries
paragraphs: A few hours after brushing, a fingernail drawn along the gumline comes away with a soft, pale smear.
For most of the twentieth century, dentistry treated it as debris whose only interesting property was that it could be scraped off.
Dental plaque is not a pile of leftovers.
It is a community with architecture, and the disease it can produce is better understood as a change in local conditions than as an invasion.
A biofilm is a population of microorganisms attached to a surface and held in a matrix that the cells themselves secrete.
In plaque that matrix is mostly polysaccharide, with protein and extracellular DNA woven through it.
It fixes cells at stable addresses and slows the movement of small molecules through the film.
It turns a smear of bacteria into a structure with an inside and an outside.
Assembly follows a reliable order.
Within minutes of a cleaning, salivary proteins adsorb onto the enamel and form the acquired pellicle, a film a fraction of a micrometer thick.
The first colonizers, mostly oral streptococci along with Actinomyces species, do not bind bare enamel at all.
They bind receptors displayed on the pellicle.
Later arrivals bind poorly to pellicle and instead attach to cells already in place.
Fusobacterium nucleatum is the great connector, able to bind both early streptococci and late colonizers that bind almost nothing else.
Sucrose holds a special place in this system.
Bacterial enzymes called glucosyltransferases split the sugar and polymerize its glucose into glucans, sticky branched polymers that make up much of the matrix.
The reaction needs no cellular energy, because the energy is already stored in the bond joining the two halves of sucrose.
Glucans glue cells to the tooth and to one another.
A sucrose-rich diet therefore does two things at once: it feeds acid production, and it builds the scaffolding that holds the acid producers against the enamel.
Because the matrix slows diffusion, a film far thinner than a millimeter develops steep internal gradients.
Oxygen is consumed near the outer surface, leaving the depths anaerobic and hospitable to organisms that could not survive in saliva.
Acid made in those depths is not immediately washed away.
Microelectrodes show that the pH inside plaque can sit more than a full unit below the pH of the saliva a millimeter away.
The consequence is the central fact of the model: the tooth surface does not experience the chemistry of the mouth but that of the film pressed against it.
Once plaque was seen as a community, the next question was which members matter.
The specific plaque hypothesis, dominant from the 1970s onward, answered that only a few do, and named Streptococcus mutans and the lactobacilli.
The case was reasonable.
Both are strongly acidogenic, making acid quickly from sugar, and aciduric, still growing at pH values that stall their neighbors.
The evidence never quite cooperated.
Lesions appear in mouths from which mutans streptococci cannot be recovered, and plenty of decay-free mouths carry them in abundance.
When sequencing replaced culturing, other capable acid producers turned up in active lesions, among them bifidobacteria and the yeast Candida albicans.
Streptococcus mutans remains a competent troublemaker and a serviceable marker of risk, but it proved neither necessary nor sufficient.
A model resting on one organism cannot absorb that many exceptions.
The ecological plaque hypothesis offered a different account.
Its claim is that local conditions decide which species dominate a site, and that caries follows a shift in those conditions rather than the arrival of a villain.
Frequent fermentable carbohydrate means frequent acid, and the acid is itself the selective pressure.
Species that tolerate low pH keep growing while acid-sensitive neighbors decline or are crowded out.
The community is plastic, and its makeup at any moment is a record of the conditions that have been acting on it.
What is lost in that shift matters as much as what is gained.
Several acid-sensitive residents are actively protective.
Some run the arginine deiminase system or produce urease, pathways that release ammonia and push local pH upward.
Others generate hydrogen peroxide that holds competitors in check.
A sustained acid challenge therefore removes brakes at the same time that it adds accelerators, which is part of why the shift tends to hold.

After sugar, plaque pH falls within minutes to a minimum of roughly 4.5 to 5.5, then climbs back toward a resting value near 6.7 as saliva buffers and clears the acid, a recovery that commonly takes twenty to sixty minutes.
Enamel begins to dissolve below a critical pH near 5.5.
Exposed root dentin, which carries less mineral, begins to dissolve closer to 6.2.
That curve explains why frequency outranks quantity.
Sweets eaten at one sitting drive the pH down once.
The same sweets nibbled across an afternoon restart the descent repeatedly and hold the film under the threshold for hours.
Underneath the microbiology sits a plain chemistry.
Enamel is about ninety-six percent mineral by weight, a form of hydroxyapatite.
When plaque fluid falls below the critical pH it is undersaturated with respect to that crystal, and mineral dissolves out of the surface.
When pH recovers and the fluid is again supersaturated, calcium and phosphate move back in.
Neither direction is an event.
Both run all day, in every mouth, and what decides the fate of a tooth is the budget, the running difference between the two.
An early lesion, the chalky white spot, is subsurface mineral loss beneath an intact surface layer, and while that layer holds, the loss can be repaid.
Saliva is the other half of the ledger.
Its bicarbonate and phosphate buffer acid, and its flow clears sugar.

It carries calcium and phosphate at levels that keep it supersaturated with respect to enamel, while statherin and proline-rich proteins keep that fluid from precipitating mineral where none is wanted.
When flow fails, through medication, radiation to the head and neck, or autoimmune disease of the glands, decay can become rapid and widespread in a person whose diet and bacteria have not changed.
Fluoride was long explained as something built into enamel during development; the part of the story that carries the most weight happens at the crystal surface, largely after the tooth has erupted.
When fluoride is present in the fluid around a crystal during recovery, it is taken up as new mineral forms, producing a fluoridated apatite that does not dissolve until roughly pH 4.5.
Lowering the threshold by about a unit shortens the part of each acid cycle in which the crystal loses ground, and fluoride also speeds repair.
What the chemistry recommends is a low concentration present often.
All of this bears on the common phrase that tooth decay is an infection a person catches.
The phrase is not entirely wrong.
Strains do move between people, and caregiver-to-infant transmission is well documented.
But the organisms involved are ordinary residents of nearly every human mouth, and their mere presence predicts very little.

Calling it an infection aims treatment at eradication, and no one can sterilize a mouth, nor would clearing out the resident community be desirable, since much of it competes with the acid makers and buffers their acid.
The more defensible statement is that the cast is already assembled, and that diet, saliva, and fluoride decide which members prosper.
The ecological account should not be oversold in its turn.
It describes a mechanism convincingly and still predicts an individual's next five years poorly.
Enamel structure, salivary flow, genetics, fluoride exposure, and the community a person started with all contribute, and no risk assessment yet separates high from low risk with confidence.
The model has earned its standing less by settling questions than by changing which questions look worth asking.
Those questions now shape practice.
If a lesion is a balance that has tipped rather than a hole, the earliest lesions are candidates for repair rather than removal, and arresting one counts as a result.
Advice shifts from scrubbing harder toward reducing how often the film is fed, keeping fluoride present, and protecting saliva.
The soft film that returns by evening is not failure but the ordinary state of a warm wet surface that is never sterile.
The useful question is not how to abolish it, but what it is being given, and how often.

questions.stem: According to the passage, the first bacteria to settle on a freshly cleaned tooth attach to
choices: glucans left behind from earlier sucrose exposure
receptors displayed on a film of adsorbed salivary proteins
strands of extracellular DNA within the plaque matrix
bare enamel crystal uncovered by the cleaning
the surfaces of Fusobacterium nucleatum cells already in place

proof.quote: do not bind bare enamel at all
They bind receptors displayed on the pellicle.

questions.why: Paragraph 3 says the first colonizers do not bind bare enamel at all. They bind receptors displayed on the acquired pellicle, the film of salivary proteins that adsorbs within minutes of a cleaning.
distractorNotes: Glucans are built later from dietary sucrose and are matrix material, not the surface the first colonizers land on.
Extracellular DNA is listed in paragraph 2 as part of the matrix, not as the attachment site for the first colonizers.
The passage says the opposite in the same sentence: those species do not bind bare enamel, which is why the pellicle matters.
That reverses the order in paragraph 3: later arrivals bind cells already in place, and Fusobacterium nucleatum is the connector between early and late groups.

questions.stem: The passage indicates that exposed root dentin begins to lose mineral
choices: only once plaque pH drops below about 4.5
near pH 6.7, the resting value of plaque
at a pH above the threshold for enamel
only where salivary flow has already failed
at the same pH as enamel, since both are apatite

proof.quote: begins to dissolve closer to 6.2
below a critical pH near 5.5

questions.why: Paragraph 10 gives two thresholds: enamel near pH 5.5 and exposed root dentin closer to 6.2. Since 6.2 is the higher number, root dentin starts dissolving earlier in the pH drop.
distractorNotes: About 4.5 is the figure from paragraph 13 for fluoridated apatite, not for root dentin.
6.7 is the resting pH plaque climbs back toward, not a point at which mineral is lost.
Paragraph 12 links failed flow to rapid decay, but paragraph 10 sets the root dentin threshold without any such condition.
The passage gives root dentin a different threshold and explains it by its lower mineral content.

questions.stem: According to the passage, bacteria can build glucans without spending cellular energy because
choices: the glucose is taken from proteins already in the pellicle
saliva supplies the phosphate the reaction consumes
the bond joining sucrose already holds the needed energy
glucosyltransferases work only in the anaerobic depths of the film
the acid released during the reaction drives the polymer forward

proof.quote: the energy is already stored in the bond joining the two halves of sucrose

questions.why: Paragraph 4 states it plainly: the reaction needs no cellular energy because the energy is already stored in the bond that joins the two halves of sucrose.
distractorNotes: The pellicle is a protein film; paragraph 4 says the glucose comes from sucrose.
Salivary phosphate appears in paragraph 12 in connection with buffering and mineral supply, not with glucan synthesis.
Anaerobic depths come from paragraph 5 and describe oxygen gradients, not the energetics of glucan building.
Acid is a separate product of sugar fermentation, and the passage never makes it the driver of glucan formation.

questions.stem: Which of the following does the passage describe as a way resident bacteria push the local pH upward?
choices: releasing ammonia through urease or arginine deiminase
generating hydrogen peroxide
polymerizing glucose from sucrose into branched glucans
consuming oxygen in the outer layer of the film
adsorbing fluoride onto the enamel crystal surface

proof.quote: pathways that release ammonia and push local pH upward

questions.why: Paragraph 9 names the arginine deiminase system and urease as pathways that release ammonia and push local pH upward.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 9 does credit some residents with hydrogen peroxide, but its stated job is holding competitors in check, not raising pH.
Glucan building is described in paragraph 4 as matrix construction, with no effect on pH given.
Oxygen consumption in paragraph 5 creates anaerobic depths; the passage ties it to which species can live there, not to pH.
Fluoride uptake belongs to paragraph 13 and is chemistry at the crystal surface rather than something the bacteria do.

questions.stem: The passage states that mineral containing fluoride resists dissolving until the pH falls to roughly

proof.quote: does not dissolve until roughly pH 4.5

questions.why: Paragraph 13 says fluoride taken up during repair produces a fluoridated apatite that does not dissolve until roughly pH 4.5, which shortens the part of each acid cycle that costs mineral.
distractorNotes: 5.0 sits inside the range plaque pH dips to after sugar, but the passage never uses it as a dissolution threshold.
5.5 is the threshold for ordinary enamel, the number fluoride improves on.
6.2 is the threshold paragraph 10 gives for exposed root dentin.
6.7 is the resting pH plaque returns to after a sugar exposure, from paragraph 10.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 8, "plastic" most nearly means
choices: able to be molded by hand into a chosen shape
made of a synthetic polymer
fixed in form once it has assembled
reshaped by the conditions acting on it
artificial rather than naturally occurring

proof.quote: The community is plastic
a record of the conditions that have been acting on it

questions.why: The sentence right after the word explains it: the community's makeup at any moment is a record of the conditions that have been acting on it. The word points to something shaped by its surroundings.
distractorNotes: This keeps the molding idea but adds someone doing the molding, while the passage credits the local conditions.
The literal material sense does not fit; the matrix described in paragraph 2 is a polysaccharide the cells make themselves.
This is the reverse of the point, since the whole paragraph describes a membership that changes as conditions change.
That is a common dictionary sense of the word, but nothing in paragraph 8 contrasts natural with artificial.

questions.stem: As used in paragraph 11, "budget" most nearly means
choices: a fixed limit on how much mineral a tooth is allowed to lose
a schedule setting when demineralization happens
the total mineral a tooth carries when it erupts
the running net balance between two opposing processes
an allowance of sugar a person can take in each day

proof.quote: the budget, the running difference between the two

questions.why: Paragraph 11 says mineral loss and mineral return both run all day, and then calls the budget the running difference between the two. It is a net balance, not a cap or a plan.
distractorNotes: A cap implies some allowance being enforced, and the passage describes a running total instead.
The passage explicitly says neither direction is an event, which rules out a set schedule.
The starting amount of mineral is not what the word tracks; the sentence is about the difference between loss and return over time.
The passage does discuss how often sugar arrives in paragraph 10, but the word here labels a mineral balance, not a diet limit.

questions.stem: The description of gradients in paragraph 5 most strongly supports which conclusion?
choices: Oxygen is absent from every layer of a mature plaque film
The species inside plaque are spread evenly through the film
Plaque must grow thicker than a millimeter before enamel is at risk
Saliva loses the ability to buffer acid once a biofilm has formed
A saliva pH reading can understate the acid at the tooth surface

proof.quote: more than a full unit below the pH of the saliva a millimeter away
the tooth surface does not experience the chemistry of the mouth

questions.why: Paragraph 5 reports that pH inside plaque can sit more than a full unit below the saliva a millimeter away, and it closes by saying the tooth meets the chemistry of the film rather than of the mouth. A saliva reading would therefore look better than conditions at the surface.
distractorNotes: Oxygen is consumed near the outer surface, which leaves the depths anaerobic; the passage does not empty the whole film of oxygen.
Gradients are the point of the paragraph, and they mean the film is not uniform.
The paragraph says the gradients form in a film far thinner than a millimeter, so thickness of that scale is not required.
Paragraphs 10 and 12 both show saliva buffering and clearing acid even though a film is present.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that an approach aimed at wiping out as much of the plaque community as possible would risk
choices: leaving enamel permanently unable to take mineral back up
converting sucrose into a form bacteria cannot use
stopping the pellicle from forming after a cleaning
removing residents that raise pH and check acid makers
raising the critical pH of enamel above 6.2

proof.quote: nor would clearing out the resident community be desirable
removes brakes at the same time that it adds accelerators

questions.why: Paragraph 9 describes acid-sensitive residents that release ammonia and hydrogen peroxide, and paragraph 14 says clearing out the resident community would not be desirable because much of it competes with the acid makers and buffers their acid.
distractorNotes: Remineralization in paragraph 11 depends on pH and on calcium and phosphate in the fluid, not on which bacteria are present.
Nothing in the passage connects removing bacteria to changing the chemistry of sucrose itself.
The pellicle is made of salivary proteins and forms within minutes of any cleaning, so bacteria are not required for it.
Critical pH is a property of the mineral in paragraph 11, and 6.2 belongs to root dentin rather than enamel.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central point of the passage?
choices: Decay reflects a shift in a resident community, not the arrival of a pathogen
Streptococcus mutans is the one organism responsible for nearly all tooth decay
Brushing the film away is the most effective defense a person has against decay
Salivary flow by itself decides whether a given tooth will decay
Fluoride has made the study of oral bacteria largely unnecessary in dentistry

proof.quote: a change in local conditions than as an invasion
rather than the arrival of a villain
diet, saliva, and fluoride decide which members prosper

questions.why: The passage moves from plaque as a structured community, through the failure of a single-organism explanation, to the ecological account and the running mineral balance it implies. The closing paragraphs make that reframing explicit.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 7 shows this claim failing, calling the organism neither necessary nor sufficient.
Paragraph 16 shifts advice away from scrubbing harder and toward how often the film is fed.
Saliva is one contributor among several, and paragraph 15 lists others that matter as well.
Fluoride gets one paragraph as surface chemistry, and the passage never sets it against studying the community.

choices: recommend that every patient be tested for Candida albicans
argue that culturing gives more reliable results than sequencing
identify the organism most useful for judging a person's risk
explain how the matrix keeps acid pressed against the enamel
show why an explanation built on one organism could not hold

proof.quote: The evidence never quite cooperated.
A model resting on one organism cannot absorb that many exceptions.

questions.why: Paragraph 7 lists findings the earlier model could not absorb: lesions without mutans streptococci, decay-free mouths full of them, and other acid producers found by sequencing. It closes by saying a model resting on one organism cannot carry that many exceptions.
distractorNotes: Candida albicans appears only in a list of acid producers, and the passage makes no testing recommendation.
The passage credits sequencing with revealing what culturing missed, which is the reverse of this claim.
The paragraph does call the organism a serviceable marker, but that is a concession made in passing, not the work the paragraph does.
That is the job of paragraph 5, not paragraph 7.

questions.stem: Which best describes how paragraphs 6 through 8 are arranged?
choices: A chemical mechanism is laid out and then applied to one patient's history
A clinical recommendation is given and then supported with laboratory measurements
A popular belief is stated and then shown to be entirely false
Two rival explanations are described and then combined into a single model
An earlier explanation is presented, tested against evidence, and replaced

proof.quote: The specific plaque hypothesis, dominant from the 1970s onward
The evidence never quite cooperated.
The ecological plaque hypothesis offered a different account.

questions.why: Paragraph 6 presents the specific plaque hypothesis and grants that its case was reasonable, paragraph 7 sets the evidence against it, and paragraph 8 supplies the ecological account in its place.
distractorNotes: The passage never follows an individual patient.
No recommendation appears in these paragraphs; advice waits until paragraph 16.
Too strong: the passage keeps Streptococcus mutans as a real troublemaker and a serviceable marker of risk.
The ecological account replaces the earlier one rather than merging with it.

questions.stem: The author's attitude toward the specific plaque hypothesis is best described as
choices: fair to its reasoning yet unconvinced
dismissive of it as careless thinking
alarmed that it still directs most treatment
eager to see it restored to favor
indifferent to whether it was ever accepted

proof.quote: The case was reasonable.
it proved neither necessary nor sufficient

questions.why: Paragraph 6 says the case was reasonable and lays out the evidence behind it, and paragraph 7 then explains calmly why that case does not cover the findings. The author gives the idea its due and still sets it aside.
distractorNotes: Too harsh: the passage says outright that the case was reasonable.
No claim is made that this model still governs treatment; paragraph 16 describes practice shaped by the newer account.
The passage moves past this model rather than arguing for its return.
The author spends two full paragraphs weighing the idea, which is not indifference.

questions.stem: In paragraph 15, the author's stance toward the ecological account is best described as
choices: neutral, since the paragraph makes no judgment either way
supportive but careful not to overstate what it can do
impatient with researchers who keep studying saliva
doubtful that it captures any real mechanism
confident that it now predicts an individual's risk accurately

proof.quote: should not be oversold in its turn
describes a mechanism convincingly and still predicts an individual's next five years poorly

questions.why: Paragraph 15 opens by warning against overselling the account, grants that it describes a mechanism convincingly, notes that it predicts an individual's next five years poorly, and credits it with changing which questions look worth asking.
distractorNotes: The paragraph offers a clear judgment: valuable, and not yet predictive.
Saliva appears in the list of contributors, and nothing in the paragraph criticizes studying it.
The same paragraph says the account describes a mechanism convincingly, so doubt about the mechanism is the wrong read.
This is the claim the paragraph explicitly denies.

questions.stem: The passage supports each of the following statements about saliva EXCEPT:
choices: It contains proteins that keep mineral from precipitating where none is wanted.
It neutralizes plaque acid about as fast as bacteria can produce it.
Its flow clears sugar from the mouth.
It carries calcium and phosphate at levels that keep it supersaturated with respect to enamel.
Its bicarbonate and phosphate buffer acid.

proof.quote: a recovery that commonly takes twenty to sixty minutes
Its bicarbonate and phosphate buffer acid
its flow clears sugar
keep it supersaturated with respect to enamel
keep that fluid from precipitating mineral where none is wanted

questions.why: Paragraph 12 supports the first four points directly. The fifth runs against the passage: paragraph 5 says acid made in the depths of the film is not immediately washed away, and paragraph 10 gives recovery times of twenty to sixty minutes.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 12 credits statherin and proline-rich proteins with exactly this, so it is supported.
Paragraph 12 states this, so it is supported and not the exception.
Paragraph 12 states this, so it is supported and not the exception.
Paragraph 12 states this, so it is supported and not the exception.

questions.stem: A reader looking for why sucrose, more than sugar in general, helps hold the film against the tooth should turn to
choices: paragraph 4
paragraph 3
paragraph 10
paragraph 2
paragraph 13

proof.quote: Sucrose holds a special place in this system.
builds the scaffolding that holds the acid producers against the enamel

questions.why: Paragraph 4 is the one that singles out sucrose, explaining how glucosyltransferases turn it into glucans that glue cells to the tooth and to one another.
distractorNotes: Paragraph 3 covers the order in which species arrive, not what diet contributes.
Paragraph 10 follows pH after a sugar exposure, which is about acid rather than attachment.
Paragraph 2 defines a biofilm and its matrix in general terms and never names a dietary sugar.
Paragraph 13 is about fluoride at the crystal surface.
